title: Understanding the Basic Structure of the Indian Constitution
author: Pendico Editorial
summary: A practical introduction to the structure, philosophy and functioning of the Constitution of India for law students and young advocates.

content.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The Constitution of India is the supreme legal framework governing the Indian State. It establishes the structure of government, distributes powers among constitutional institutions and guarantees fundamental rights to individuals.
For a law student, constitutional law is not merely an academic subject. Constitutional principles frequently appear in litigation before the Supreme Court and High Courts.

content.heading: Why the Constitution Matters
paragraphs: Every legislation, executive action and governmental decision must operate within the constitutional framework.
The Constitution therefore acts as both a source of governmental authority and a limitation on governmental power.

content.heading: Fundamental Rights
paragraphs: Part III of the Constitution contains Fundamental Rights. These rights protect individual liberty and impose constitutional limitations on State action.
Articles 14, 19 and 21 are particularly important in constitutional litigation and have been interpreted extensively by the Supreme Court.

content.heading: Judicial Review
paragraphs: Judicial review enables constitutional courts to examine the legality and constitutionality of legislative and executive action.
The power of judicial review is closely connected with constitutional supremacy and the protection of fundamental rights.

content.heading: For Law Students
paragraphs: A strong constitutional-law foundation requires regular reading of the constitutional text together with leading Supreme Court judgments.
Students should learn to identify the constitutional provision involved, the issue before the Court, the ratio decidendi and the practical impact of the judgment.

keyTakeaways: The Constitution is the supreme law of India.
Fundamental Rights impose important limitations on State action.
Constitutional courts exercise judicial review.
Understanding constitutional provisions requires reading leading judgments.

title: How to Read a Supreme Court Judgment Like a Lawyer
author: Pendico Editorial
summary: A practical method for reading lengthy Supreme Court judgments efficiently and extracting the principles that actually matter.

content.heading: Do Not Read Every Judgment Like a Textbook
paragraphs: Judgments can contain extensive factual backgrounds, submissions of counsel, precedents, statutory provisions and reasoning. A lawyer must learn to identify the legally decisive portions.
The first objective should be to understand what question the Court was required to decide.

content.heading: Step 1 — Identify the Facts
paragraphs: Read the factual background carefully enough to understand the dispute.
Do not spend excessive time memorising facts that have no relevance to the legal principle.

content.heading: Step 2 — Identify the Issues
paragraphs: Ask: What precise legal question was before the Court?
An issue should preferably be expressed as a legal question rather than a general description of the dispute.

content.heading: Step 3 — Find the Statutory Provisions
paragraphs: Identify every important constitutional provision, section, rule or regulation considered by the Court.
Read the statutory language independently before analysing the Court's interpretation.

content.heading: Step 4 — Identify the Ratio
paragraphs: The ratio decidendi is the legal principle necessary for the decision.
A lawyer should distinguish the ratio from factual observations, background discussion and arguments advanced by counsel.

content.heading: Step 5 — Note the Final Order
paragraphs: Always read the operative portion of the judgment.
The final relief granted or refused determines the immediate legal result of the litigation.

keyTakeaways: Start with the legal issue.
Identify the governing statutory provisions.
Separate arguments from the Court's reasoning.
Identify the ratio decidendi.
Always read the final order.

title: BNS, BNSS and BSA: Understanding India's New Criminal Laws
author: Pendico Editorial
summary: An introductory guide to the three major criminal-law enactments that replaced the former IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act framework.

content.heading: The Three New Criminal Laws
paragraphs: India introduced three major criminal-law enactments: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.
Together, these statutes address substantive criminal offences, criminal procedure and the law of evidence.

content.heading: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
paragraphs: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita deals primarily with substantive criminal offences and punishments.
For criminal practitioners, understanding the ingredients of each offence remains fundamental to drafting complaints, bail applications, discharge applications and trial strategy.

content.heading: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita
paragraphs: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita governs criminal procedure.
It is particularly important for advocates dealing with FIRs, investigation, arrest, remand, bail, investigation reports, trials and appeals.

content.heading: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam
paragraphs: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam deals with evidentiary principles.
Evidence law determines what material may be legally relied upon and how courts evaluate relevant evidence.

content.heading: Practical Importance
paragraphs: A young criminal lawyer should study all three statutes together rather than treating them as isolated subjects.
A criminal case often requires simultaneous analysis of the offence, procedural provision and evidentiary foundation.

keyTakeaways: BNS primarily deals with offences and punishments.
BNSS primarily deals with criminal procedure.
BSA deals with evidence.
Criminal litigation requires understanding the interaction between all three.

title: How to Build a Strong Legal Research Habit
author: Pendico Editorial
summary: A practical system for law students who want to become faster and more accurate legal researchers.

content.heading: Start With the Legal Question
paragraphs: Legal research should begin with a precise legal question rather than a broad search.
The narrower the question, the easier it becomes to identify relevant legislation and precedents.

content.heading: Use Primary Sources
paragraphs: Whenever possible, begin with legislation, constitutional provisions and judgments.
Secondary sources are useful for orientation, but the final legal position should be verified against authoritative primary material.

content.heading: Create a Case Note
paragraphs: For every important judgment, record the facts, issues, provisions, arguments, reasoning, ratio and final order.
This creates a personal case-law database that becomes increasingly valuable during internships and practice.

keyTakeaways: Begin with a precise legal question.
Prioritise primary legal sources.
Maintain structured case notes.
Verify important propositions before relying on them.

title: The Indian Judicial System Explained
author: Pendico Editorial
summary: An accessible overview of India's judicial hierarchy and the role of the Supreme Court, High Courts and subordinate courts.

content.heading: Supreme Court of India
paragraphs: The Supreme Court is the highest constitutional court in India.
It exercises original, appellate and advisory jurisdiction in accordance with the Constitution and applicable law.

content.heading: High Courts
paragraphs: High Courts operate at the State or territorial level and exercise constitutional, appellate, supervisory and other jurisdictions conferred by law.
For advocates practising in Tamil Nadu, the Madras High Court is particularly important.

content.heading: Subordinate Judiciary
paragraphs: District and subordinate courts handle a large volume of civil and criminal litigation.
These courts are often where advocates develop the practical skills required for trial advocacy.

content.heading: Why Young Lawyers Should Understand Court Structure
paragraphs: Knowing jurisdiction is essential when deciding where a proceeding should be instituted or challenged.
A good advocate must understand territorial jurisdiction, pecuniary jurisdiction, subject-matter jurisdiction and appellate routes.

keyTakeaways: The Supreme Court is India's apex court.
High Courts exercise important constitutional and appellate jurisdiction.
Subordinate courts form the foundation of day-to-day litigation.
Jurisdiction is a fundamental advocacy skill.

title: What Makes a Good Advocate?
author: Pendico Editorial
summary: The essential professional habits that law students should develop before entering litigation practice.

content.heading: Legal Knowledge Is Only the Foundation
paragraphs: A practising advocate requires more than knowledge of statutes and judgments.
Drafting, oral advocacy, client communication, procedural knowledge and professional discipline are equally important.

content.heading: Courtroom Discipline
paragraphs: Young advocates should observe courtroom procedure carefully and learn how matters are called, mentioned, argued and adjourned.
Professional courtesy toward judges, opponents and court staff is an essential part of practice.

content.heading: Drafting Skills
paragraphs: Clear drafting is one of the most valuable skills an advocate can develop.
A strong pleading should identify the relevant facts, legal grounds and relief sought without unnecessary repetition.

content.heading: Continuous Learning
paragraphs: Law changes continuously through legislation, judgments and procedural developments.
A serious advocate therefore treats legal research as a permanent professional habit.

keyTakeaways: Develop drafting and oral advocacy together.
Observe courtroom procedure.
Maintain professional discipline.
Keep learning throughout practice.
